bibl.title: Pottery from the Early Roman Rubbish Dumps in Berenike, Egypt. Notes on the Material from Trenches 96/14 and 107/15.
bibl.seg: Agnieszka Dzwonek, Pottery from the Early Roman Rubbish Dumps in Berenike, Egypt. Notes on the Material from Trenches 96/14 and 107/15.

Grażyna Bąkowska-Czerner & Rafał Czerner (edd.), Greco-Roman Cities at the Crossroads of Cultures. The 20th Anniversary of Polish-Egyptian Conservation Mission Marina el-Alamein (Oxford, 2019) pp. 96-102, figg.
bibl.note: Berenike was a port city established in Ptolemaic times on the Red Sea Coast and functioned until the Late Roman Period. Archaeological excavations of the site yielded a great deal of ceramic material, the majority of which came from trash deposits. Aims to illustrate the abundance of such material by taking as examples trenches 96 and 107, two out of several trenches dug in the area of the early Roman rubbish dumps. The registered pottery consists mostly of Egyptian amphorae and locally produced table and cooking ware with a large amount of imported wares from many regions of the Roman Empire. What clearly differentiates the Berenike assemblage is, however, the presence of pottery from South Arabia, Eritrea and India, which highlights the flourishing trade with Arabia, Africa and the Far East at that time.
